subject: physics
title: Hubble's Law and Age of the Universe
welcome_lead: Plot v against d and read off H₀ — then estimate the universe's age as 1/H₀.
meta_desc: A-Level Cosmology adventure on Hubble's law, H₀ and the age of the universe.
final_note: 1/H₀ gives a rough age, but accelerating expansion makes the true age different.

concepts.def: v = H₀ d for distant galaxies.
Known L source for distance, e.g. type Ia SN.

walkthroughs.body_html: Plotting recession velocity (from z) against distance yields straight line through origin; gradient is H₀. Bigger H₀ means faster expansion now.
If expansion has been constant, time since Big Bang ≈ 1/H₀. With H₀ ≈ 2.3 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹, T ≈ 4.4 × 10¹⁷ s ≈ 14 billion years.
Need d to test Hubble's law. Cepheids and type Ia supernovae are standard candles: known L means measured flux gives d.

mcqs.q: What is the currently accepted age of the universe?
options: About 6 billion years, the same as the Earth.
Light-years — it's a measure of cosmic distance.
About 14 billion years — close enough for any purpose.

mcqs.q: What are typical units for the Hubble constant?
options: Light-years — it's a measure of cosmic distance.
Metres per second — it's the speed at which the universe expands.
The galaxies are turning red because they are getting older.
km per second per megaparsec (km/s/Mpc) — recession speed per unit distance.

mcqs.q: What does the cosmological redshift of distant galaxies indicate?
options: Light-years — it's a measure of cosmic distance.
Space itself is expanding, stretching the wavelength of light from distant galaxies as it travels.
Galaxies are moving through space away from us, like objects flying outward from a centre.
The galaxies are turning red because they are getting older.

options: Known L source for distance, e.g. type Ia SN.
